name: Aruba Ariba
description: Aruba's signature pour: vodka, rum, crème de banana and the island's own Coecoei liqueur, layered orange and red over crushed ice.
funFact: Coecoei is made on Aruba from the fermented sap of the agave-like kukwisa plant, and it is what makes an authentic Aruba Ariba impossible to reproduce properly off the island.

steps: Shake the vodka, rum, crème de banana and the juices with ice.
Pour into a hurricane glass filled with crushed ice.
Float the Coecoei over the top so it streaks red through the orange.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Goombay Smash
description: The Abacos' most guarded secret: coconut rum, dark rum, pineapple and apricot, in a recipe the original bar has never fully written down.
funFact: Miss Emily's Blue Bee Bar on Green Turtle Cay invented it in the 1960s and has kept the exact proportions in the family ever since; every other version in the Bahamas is a reconstruction.

steps: Add the coconut rum, apricot brandy, pineapple juice and lemon juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds and strain into an ice-filled highball glass.
Float the dark rum over the top.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a cherry.

name: Sky Juice
description: Gin and coconut water with sweetened condensed milk and nutmeg — Bahamian breakfast, sold from roadside stalls before the sun is fully up.
funFact: Also called 'gully wash', it is traditional at Junkanoo — the Bahamian street parade that runs through the small hours of Boxing Day and New Year's Day.

steps: Whisk the condensed milk into the coconut water until fully dissolved.
Add the gin and stir.
Pour over ice into a cup or jar.
Grate fresh nutmeg generously over the top.

name: Yellow Bird
description: Rum, Galliano and banana liqueur over citrus — sunshine yellow, named for the calypso standard that plays on loop across the islands.
funFact: The song 'Yellow Bird' is an adaptation of an 1880s Haitian melody; the cocktail borrowed the name in the 1960s when Galliano was on every back bar in the Caribbean.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake for about 12 seconds.
Strain into a chilled coupe, or over fresh ice in a highball.
Garnish with an orange wheel.

name: Bajan Rum Punch
description: The rhyme, sung the Barbadian way: sour, sweet, strong, weak, with Angostura across the top and nutmeg over that.
funFact: Barbados claims the rhyme as its own national verse, and adds a fifth line most islands leave off: 'a dash of bitters and a sprinkle of spice'.

steps: Combine the lime juice, sugar syrup, rum and water in a jug in that order.
Stir well and chill thoroughly — punch should never be shaken to order.
Pour over ice into rocks glasses.
Dash Angostura generously over each glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top.

name: Corn 'n' Oil
description: Barbadian and barely diluted: dark rum, falernum and lime, stirred until it looks like crude oil in the glass. Clove, almond and molasses.
funFact: Falernum is a Barbadian invention — a low-proof syrup-liqueur of lime, clove, almond and ginger — and this is the drink it exists for. The name describes the drink's dark, slick appearance.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with crushed ice.
Add the falernum and lime juice.
Pour the rum over the top and stir briefly with a swizzle stick.
Dash the Angostura across the surface.
Garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Rum Swizzle
description: Bermuda's national drink and the reason swizzle sticks exist: black rum, falernum and juices churned over crushed ice until the glass frosts.
funFact: The Swizzle Inn near the airport has been serving it since 1932 under the slogan 'Swizzle Inn, Swagger Out'; the swizzle stick itself comes from the forked branch of the Caribbean Quararibea tree.

steps: Fill a tall glass or a small pitcher with crushed ice.
Add all the ingredients.
Spin a swizzle stick between your palms until the outside of the glass frosts over.
Top with more crushed ice to refill the glass.
Garnish with an orange slice and a cherry.

name: Canchánchara
description: The oldest Cuban drink of them all: raw cane spirit, honey and lime, served in a clay cup. Rougher than the Daiquiri and considerably older.
funFact: Cuban independence fighters, the mambises, drank it in the 1860s as a field ration and a cold remedy; the bar La Canchánchara in Trinidad still serves it in the traditional earthenware cups.

ingredients.item: Aguardiente de caña or white rum

steps: Stir the honey and cold water together in the bottom of a clay cup until the honey loosens.
Add the lime juice and stir again.
Pour in the cane spirit and add cracked ice.
Stir until the outside of the cup is cold, and serve with the spoon still in it.

name: El Presidente
description: Havana's aristocrat: aged rum stirred with blanc vermouth, curaçao and a whisper of grenadine. Silk where the Daiquiri is citrus.
funFact: Named for Cuban president Gerardo Machado and the drink of choice for the American upper class who fled Prohibition to Havana — Basil Woon called it 'the aristocrat of cocktails' in 1928.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a mixing glass with ice.
Stir for about 25 seconds until well chilled and properly diluted.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange twist over the surface and drop it in.

name: Havana Special
description: A Daiquiri that took a detour through the pineapple fields: rum, pineapple juice and maraschino, shaken to a pale gold froth.
funFact: Recorded in Havana's Sloppy Joe's bar menu in the 1930s — a bar so central to American drinking tourism that its cocktail list was sold as a souvenir booklet.

steps: Add all the ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a pineapple leaf or a cherry.

name: Mary Pickford
description: Pink, pineapple-bright and named for a silent film star: white rum, pineapple, maraschino and grenadine, invented while Hollywood was drinking out its Prohibition exile.
funFact: Created at the Hotel Sevilla-Biltmore in Havana in the 1920s for Mary Pickford, who was in Cuba filming with Douglas Fairbanks and Charlie Chaplin.

steps: Add all ingredients to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for about 12 seconds — fresh pineapple juice needs the aeration.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a maraschino cherry.

name: Mulata
description: A Daiquiri built on aged rum and crème de cacao — chocolate and lime, which should not work and completely does.
funFact: Created at Havana's Floridita, the same bar that made the Daiquiri famous; 'mulata' refers to the drink's brown-gold colour once the cacao and aged rum combine.

steps: Add all ingredients to a blender with a scoop of crushed ice, or shake hard with cubed ice.
Blend or shake until frosty.
Pour into a chilled coupe.
Grate a little dark chocolate over the top.

name: Saoco
description: Rum and coconut water, straight from the nut. The Piña Colada's lean, unsweetened ancestor — and far better on a genuinely hot day.
funFact: Traditionally the top is macheted off a green coconut, rum is poured straight in, and the whole thing is drunk from the shell — the coconut meat is scooped out afterwards.

steps: If using a coconut, cut a wide opening in the top and pour off a little water to make room.
Add the rum and lime juice directly to the coconut or to an ice-filled highball glass.
Top with coconut water.
Stir once and drink through a straw.
recipe.garnish: A lime wedge, or nothing at all

name: Santo Libre
description: The Cuba Libre's lighter neighbour: white rum, lime and lemon-lime soda instead of cola. Crisper, and easier in the afternoon.
funFact: Named in deliberate contrast to the Cuba Libre — the Dominican version swaps the cola for Sprite or 7-Up, which locals argue lets the rum actually taste like rum.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Add the rum and lime juice.
Top with cold lemon-lime soda.
Stir once gently and garnish with a lime wedge.

name: Kremas
description: Haiti's Christmas in a bottle: rhum, coconut cream, condensed milk, lime zest and spice, thick enough to coat the glass.
funFact: Also spelled cremas or kremasi, it is the drink of Haitian holidays and diaspora gatherings — and every family insists their version is the correct one, usually over the amount of star anise.

steps: Warm the coconut cream gently with the spices and lime zest, then cool completely.
Blend the spiced coconut cream with the condensed milk, evaporated milk and vanilla until smooth.
Stir in the rhum — never blend it in hot, or the texture breaks.
Strain into bottles and refrigerate for at least 24 hours before drinking.
Serve very cold in small glasses; it keeps for weeks.

name: Bob Marley
description: Red, gold and green in a shot glass — grenadine, banana liqueur and melon, layered so the flag holds. More about the pour than the palate.
funFact: The layers work because of sugar density: grenadine is heaviest and sinks, melon liqueur is lightest and floats — pour in the wrong order and you get a muddy brown shot.

steps: Pour the grenadine into the bottom of a shot glass.
Float the banana liqueur over the back of a barspoon so it settles on top of the grenadine.
Float the melon liqueur the same way to make the top layer.
Serve immediately without stirring.

name: Dirty Banana
description: A frozen banana milkshake that went to Negril and came back with rum and coffee liqueur. Resort poolside, distilled.
funFact: It is the default poolside order across Jamaica's north coast, and the reason most Jamaican hotel bars keep a dedicated blender running from mid-morning.

steps: Put the banana, milk, rum, coffee liqueur and banana liqueur into a blender.
Add the ice and blend until completely smooth.
Pour into a hurricane glass.
Garnish with a banana slice and a dusting of grated chocolate.

name: Planter's Punch
description: One of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak — the rhyme that built Caribbean punch, poured long over crushed ice with nutmeg on top.
funFact: The rhyme predates the cocktail glass: 'one of sour, two of sweet, three of strong, four of weak' appears in Caribbean sources from the 1800s and still governs rum punch across the islands.

steps: Combine the rum, lime juice, sugar syrup and water in a shaker with ice.
Shake briefly, about 8 seconds.
Pour unstrained into a tall glass and top with more crushed ice.
Dash the Angostura over the top so it bleeds down through the ice.
Grate fresh nutmeg over the surface.
recipe.garnish: Freshly grated nutmeg and an orange slice

name: Ting with a Sting
description: Jamaica's whole cocktail culture in two words: Ting grapefruit soda, white overproof rum, ice. The sting is not a metaphor.
funFact: Ting has been bottled in Jamaica since 1976 and is deliberately bitter; the 'sting' is traditionally Wray & Nephew White Overproof, which runs at 63% ABV.

steps: Fill a highball glass with ice.
Pour in the overproof rum and the lime juice.
Top with cold Ting.
Stir once and garnish with a grapefruit or lime wedge.

name: Planteur
description: The French Antilles' planter's punch: rhum agricole with mango, guava and passionfruit, softer and more perfumed than its English-speaking cousin.
funFact: Rhum agricole is distilled from fresh cane juice rather than molasses, which is why a Planteur tastes grassy and vegetal where a Jamaican punch tastes of treacle.

steps: Combine all ingredients in a shaker with ice.
Shake for 10 seconds.
Pour into an ice-filled highball glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top and garnish with a lime wheel.

name: Bilí
description: Vieques in a bottle: pitorro steeped for months with quenepas, cinnamon and sugar until the moonshine turns sweet, fruity and deceptively smooth.
funFact: Bilí is a Vieques speciality made with quenepas (Spanish limes) and is traditionally buried or hidden to age — families open bottles at Christmas that were sealed the previous summer.

steps: Put the peeled quenepas, cinnamon, sugar and vanilla into a large sealable jar.
Cover with the pitorro and seal tightly.
Store somewhere dark and cool for at least two months, turning the jar occasionally.
Strain into bottles, leaving the fruit behind.
Serve chilled in small measures.

name: Chichaíto
description: Two ingredients, no mercy: pitorro and anisette, shaken with ice and served cold enough to hide how strong it is.
funFact: A staple of Puerto Rican Christmas parrandas, where it is carried house to house in a bottle kept in the freezer — the sugar content stops it from freezing solid.

steps: Combine the pitorro and anisette in a shaker with plenty of ice.
Shake hard for 10 seconds to chill and slightly dilute.
Strain into chilled shot glasses.
Serve immediately, ice cold.

name: Coco Loco
description: Served in the coconut it was made from: rum, coconut cream and whatever tropical juice is closest to hand, blended into holiday shorthand.
funFact: The 'loco' is usually the pour — beach vendors from Luquillo to Loíza free-pour three spirits into the same coconut and stop when it looks about right.

steps: Cut the top off a young coconut and pour the water into a blender.
Add the rums, coconut cream, pineapple juice, lime and crushed ice.
Blend until smooth and slushy.
Pour back into the coconut shell and serve with a straw.
recipe.garnish: Pineapple wedge and a paper umbrella

name: Sorrel
description: Christmas red: hibiscus calyces steeped with clove, ginger and orange peel, sweetened and cut with rum. Tart, spiced and unmistakably festive.
funFact: The sorrel plant is a hibiscus relative that fruits right at Christmas across the Caribbean, which is precisely why the drink became a December tradition from Trinidad to Jamaica.

steps: Put the sorrel, ginger, cloves and orange peel in a large heatproof jug.
Pour over the boiling water, cover, and leave to steep for at least 12 hours.
Strain out the solids and stir in the sugar until dissolved.
Add the rum to taste and refrigerate.
Serve very cold over ice.
